label: Chapter 4: A Grand Duchy Is Born, 1815 to 1867

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Picture the scene. Vienna, the winter of 1814 and 1815.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Napoleon has been defeated and exiled.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The diplomats of Europe, kings, princes, and ministers in glittering uniforms, gather for the Congress of Vienna to redraw the map.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Their main goal is simple. Make sure France can never again conquer its neighbors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And one way to do that is to put something strong on France's northern border.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. So they combine the Netherlands and Belgium into a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, ruled by William of Orange-Nassau, who became King William the First.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Luxembourg?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: William's family had lost its ancestral German lands, so the great powers looked for ways to compensate him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of them was Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Nine. Owner count, nine.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they made it a state in its own right.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They raised it to the rank of grand duchy, a way of saying it was more than an ordinary duchy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A proper sovereign state, with a seat in the new German Confederation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, so what's a grand duchy, practically?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is it like a duchy, but with better snacks?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ha. No. It's a duchy with a promotion.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And William would be both King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A so-called personal union, in which the same man wore two crowns over two countries that were otherwise separate.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Two hats, one head.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two hats, one head. And that's 1815.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Grand Duchy of Luxembourg came into being, and it remains the only grand duchy in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But it was smaller than the old duchy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Much smaller. Prussia, the rising power on the Rhine, demanded land, and Luxembourg lost its entire eastern border region, the territory east of the rivers Moselle, Sûre, and Our.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: About a quarter of its area.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's the second time it had been carved up?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the modern era, yes. And the fortress became a fortress of the German Confederation, and a Prussian garrison moved in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Grand Duke ruled the country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Prussians held the rock.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So who actually owned it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Depends who you asked, and on which day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'll count the Prussians as tenants.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wise.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then, 1830. The great shock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In Brussels, riots broke out after an opera performance.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within weeks, the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands had risen up in revolution.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They were Catholic and mostly French-speaking, and they resented rule by a Protestant, Dutch-speaking king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They declared independence as the new Kingdom of Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A revolution after an opera. That's very Belgian.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Luxembourg joined in. Most Luxembourgers took part in the uprising, sent representatives to the Belgian national congress, and for several years almost the whole country was governed from Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The only exception was the capital, where the Prussian garrison held the fortress firmly in the name of the German Confederation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it was unresolved.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For nearly a decade. Belgium claimed all of it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Dutch king claimed all of it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great powers met in London and eventually proposed a compromise.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1839, after King William finally accepted defeat, a treaty was signed in London that carved the country in two.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who got what?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The western part of Luxembourg, the French-speaking part, went to Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It included the towns of Arlon and Bastogne, a name we'll meet again in the Second World War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That was roughly sixty-five percent of the country's territory and about half its population, something like one hundred and seventy-five thousand people.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Sixty-five percent. That's not a trim.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a haircut with a lawnmower.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ha. What remained was the eastern, German-speaking part, essentially the Luxembourg of today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How was it decided?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The line was drawn in London, using maps that were out of date and inaccurate, by diplomats who had never visited the places they were dividing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Never visited. Wow.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To compensate the German Confederation for the loss, part of the Dutch province of Limburg was attached to it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, which had been a middling European territory, became a small, landlocked, mostly poor country, with about one hundred and seventy thousand inhabitants.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's rough.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But there's a twist. The treaty of 1839 is often described as the moment Luxembourg's independence began, because it fixed the borders.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the first time there was a clear, internationally recognized line around a state called Luxembourg, the same line you can cross on a bridge or a country road today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a tragic loss, but it was also a beginning.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So how were the decades that followed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Hard. Luxembourg was a farming country with little industry, and in the eighteen-forties, a potato blight and poor harvests pushed many families into hunger.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1842, the Grand Duchy joined the German customs union, the Zollverein, which tied its economy to the German states and opened up markets for its goods.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it also meant that Luxembourg's economic fate was linked to its neighbor across the Moselle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And people left.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between about 1840 and 1890, tens of thousands of Luxembourgers emigrated.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many went to the United States and settled in the Midwest, especially in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, and the area around Chicago.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a country of fewer than two hundred thousand people, it was an enormous drain.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, the country was learning to govern itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1841, William the Second, the king who followed William the First, granted Luxembourg its first constitution, creating an assembly of the estates.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1848, the year revolutions shook Europe, a more liberal constitution followed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Dutch kings were fully engaged?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not very. William the Third, who ruled from 1849, rarely visited.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Day to day, the country was run by his brother Prince Henry as his representative.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Another absentee landlord.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Some things don't change. And then, a national consciousness woke up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Writers and poets began composing in Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect that ordinary people spoke at home and that had no official status.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did they write?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1859, the poet Michel Lentz wrote a song Luxembourgers still sing, called the Feierwon, the Fire Wagon, about the arrival of the railway.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its refrain became the national motto.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We want to remain what we are.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: After nine changes of owner, that is a bold line.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. In the same decade, Lentz wrote the words of the song that would become the national anthem, Ons Heemecht, which means Our Homeland.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was officially adopted in 1895.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1872, Michel Rodange published Renert, a long satirical poem in Luxembourgish about a crafty fox, which many people consider the country's national epic.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A national epic about a fox. I respect that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now we come to the crisis that nearly started a war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh no.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1866, Prussia defeated Austria in a short, decisive war, and the German Confederation, which had existed since 1815, was dissolved.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Suddenly no one was sure what Luxembourg's status was.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Was it part of Germany? Was it independent?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And who owned the fortress, with its Prussian garrison?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Napoleon the Third saw an opportunity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Prussia had just become dramatically more powerful, and he wanted something in return to keep the balance, and to restore French prestige.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He offered to buy Luxembourg from King William the Third of the Netherlands, who was short of money and had little emotional attachment to the place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. He tried to buy a country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He did.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What was the price?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: William agreed to the idea in principle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it was basically a garage sale for a fortress.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ha. Just about. But then, Bismarck.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Prussian chancellor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Otto von Bismarck was not going to let France take a strategic fortress on the German frontier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He made sure that news of the sale leaked, and German public opinion exploded.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg is German soil, politicians and newspapers cried.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And for a few weeks in the spring of 1867, Europe stood at the edge of war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Over Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How did it end?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Diplomacy won. The great powers met in London in May of 1867, and agreed on a settlement that satisfied everyone and no one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The second Treaty of London, signed on the eleventh of May, declared that Luxembourg was an independent state, under the sovereignty of the House of Orange-Nassau, and that it would be perpetually neutral, under the collective guarantee of the great powers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Perpetually neutral. I bet that works out well.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We'll get there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the fortress?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Prussian garrison would leave.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the fortress, the Gibraltar of the North, would be dismantled, so that no one could use it as a weapon against their neighbors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So Napoleon the Third didn't get it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He didn't. So, for the owner count, an almost.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: An almost doesn't count.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. Still nine.
